symptoms: Olive-green to black velvety spots on leaves and fruit. Leaves may yellow and drop early.
favoured_by: Cool, wet spring weather with long periods of leaf wetness.
cultural_practices: Rake up and destroy fallen leaves in autumn. Prune for airflow. Plant scab-resistant varieties where possible.

symptoms: Purple-edged leaf spots that turn brown in the centre, like a frog's eye. Rotting fruit and cankers on branches.
cultural_practices: Prune out dead wood and cankers. Remove shrivelled fruit from the tree and the ground.

symptoms: Bright yellow-orange spots on the upper leaf, later with small tube-like growths underneath.
favoured_by: Wet spring weather. Needs nearby juniper or cedar trees to complete its life cycle.
cultural_practices: Remove nearby junipers where practical. Plant resistant varieties.

symptoms: Long, narrow, rectangular grey to tan spots running between the leaf veins.
favoured_by: Warm (25–30 °C), very humid weather with heavy dew, and crop residue left on the field.
cultural_practices: Rotate with a non-maize crop. Bury or remove crop residue. Use tolerant hybrids.

symptoms: Small, powdery, cinnamon-brown pustules on both sides of the leaf.
favoured_by: Mild temperatures (16–23 °C) with high humidity or dew.
cultural_practices: Plant resistant hybrids. Early sowing helps the crop avoid the worst infection period.

cultural_practices: Rotate crops and manage residue. Use resistant hybrids.

symptoms: Tan leaf spots with dark edges and tiny black dots. Berries shrivel into hard black mummies.
favoured_by: Warm, wet weather in spring and early summer.
cultural_practices: Remove mummified berries and infected canes. Keep the canopy open for airflow.

symptoms: Yellow or red stripes between the leaf veins, dark spots on berries, and rotting wood inside the trunk.
favoured_by: Pruning wounds that let fungi into the wood, and drought stress.
cultural_practices: Prune in dry weather and protect large cuts. Remove badly infected vines. No spray cures it.

symptoms: Irregular dark brown spots on older leaves, which may dry out and fall.
cultural_practices: Remove fallen infected leaves. Open up the canopy for airflow.

pathogen: Candidatus Liberibacter (bacterium), spread by the Asian citrus psyllid
symptoms: Blotchy, uneven yellowing of leaves that doesn't match on both sides of the vein. Small, lopsided, bitter fruit.
favoured_by: Spread by psyllid insects, which are most active in warm weather.
cultural_practices: There is no cure. Remove infected trees to protect the rest. Control psyllids and plant certified disease-free saplings. Report suspected cases to your agriculture officer.
